prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B020 prize for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Round 1 showed that all six of us reach the same trio, and the chair is right that what remains is attribution and wording, not merit. The science is complete: the incretin effect and proglucagon processing, the identity of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, receptor biology, and a drug class with randomized outcome-trial benefit in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. Each discovery step has a distinct academic owner. I answer the chair's questions as follows. A single part is preferable to two parts, because adding a second achievement would force us to cut a core GLP-1 name, and I will not trade a defensible attribution for breadth. The citation should honour discovery and physiology, with the therapy named only as the consequence, so that no wording assigns priority between Mojsov and Habener beyond identifying the active form. The long-term safety questions for the obesity indication are real but they concern the use of a validated mechanism, not the discovery, so I would not change the wording or the timing because of them.
statement.case_against: The credit is still the weak point and I have not found a way to remove that weakness. I cannot settle Mojsov versus Habener from the supplied record, and the three-person limit leaves out Knudsen, whose long-acting analogues are what reached patients. If a majority decides the achievement is the therapy rather than the hormone system, then Knudsen should be considered and my configuration would be the wrong one, but then the committee must say which of Mojsov or Drucker she replaces and why, and no argument made so far gives a reason that I find convincing. A prize built on physiology also risks being read as undervaluing drug development. I accept that cost knowingly, because the alternative blurs a discovery prize with an industrial development award.

responses.point: Sandberg moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to the Mojsov trio, but still doubts that a single-achievement prize is the best use of the committee's range, considers B045 and B040 strong enough for a shared prize, and says Knudsen is not left out merely for space.
responses.response: I welcome the move to the discovery trio and I agree with you that if the committee prefers to honour the drug, it should say so openly and not by default. On range, I do not think a prize needs to span two fields to be a good use of the committee's judgment. B045 and B040 are not ready to be paired with B020 on the names we have: any three-name split of optogenetics excludes someone with a decisive claim, and CAR-T leaves out Eshhar. A second part would also require trimming the GLP-1 trio, which would damage the best attribution on the list. I am therefore holding B020 alone, and I remain open to B045 or B040 in a later year when credit has been settled.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would keep Knudsen only in the citation text if the committee prefers a physiology-plus-translation framing, would drop the contested name and not the physiologist, and ranks optogenetics below the immunology and oncology candidates because of limited clinical translation and unresolved six-way credit.
responses.response: I agree with her on keeping the physiologist. I would not name Knudsen in the citation text, because that gives her recognition in words while excluding her from the prize, and I think this would invite more criticism than it prevents. On optogenetics I agree that unresolved credit is the main obstacle. I would add that the case for a method prize does not depend on patient benefit. This prize has honoured enabling methods when their effect on biology was decisive, and optogenetics clearly meets that bar for circuit dissection, though that is a separate question from whether the names are ready. Her fallback of B034 also remains unanswered on my earlier question: who first showed TNF to be dominant upstream in the synovium, and is the Feldmann and Maini contribution more than clinical proof of concept? Until that is shown I keep B034 below B045 and B040.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds that Hegemann was as decisive as Nagel for channelrhodopsin, that my round-1 optogenetics trio of Boyden, Nagel and Deisseroth omitted him, and that he would want this resolved before treating B045 as ready.
responses.response: The criticism is correct. Hegemann's characterisation of channelrhodopsin is on a par with Nagel's, and a trio of Boyden, Nagel and Deisseroth cannot be defended on that basis. In my view this is a structural problem, because the discovery of the light-gated channel (Bamberg, Nagel, Hegemann), the neuronal deployment (Boyden, Deisseroth) and Miesenboeck's earlier genetic targeting each have a strong claim and no three-person subset covers them fairly. I therefore stop treating B045 as a prize I could propose and keep it only as an alternative. I agree with you on Rosenberg for B040: June and Sadelain is the cleanest pair, though Eshhar's absence from the list remains a problem I cannot fix.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that Knudsen's engineering is medicinal chemistry building on a discovered mechanism, that the Mojsov priority question calls for care in the citation wording and not removal of her, and that the committee should not hold the prize back by relitigating attribution beyond what the evidence can settle.
responses.response: I agree with all three points and I have adopted the last one in my wording. Because the priority between Mojsov and Habener cannot be settled from the file, the citation says 'the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form', which credits identification and characterisation of the active form without asserting who was first. That is the most that this record supports. I differ with you only on how much delay costs: because the field is mature, further delay mostly risks mis-allocation, but a hasty prize with an overstated priority claim would be worse, so care in wording is the right place to spend our effort and not in widening the trio.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, keeps Mojsov in the third place while accepting that this is contestable, would not oppose reconsidering if colleagues find the therapeutic framing more persuasive, and raises the long-term safety and durability of the obesity indication.
responses.response: I think the third place is correct and I have looked for a reason to reconsider it. A therapy-framed prize would have to drop either Mojsov or Drucker for Knudsen. Mojsov defined the active peptide on which the drug programmes depended, and Drucker's receptor biology and translational pharmacology link the physiology to the clinic, so I cannot find a defensible name to remove. On safety, I accept that durability data for obesity are still accumulating. But the same is true of many medicines after a Nobel recognition, and the evidence for the mechanism and for outcome benefit in diabetes and cardiovascular and renal disease is already strong. I would leave the safety question out of the citation, and not add a hedge that suggests the discovery itself is in doubt.

uncertainties: Whether Habener or other early contributors have a priority claim on the active GLP-1 peptide that would displace Mojsov; the supplied record does not settle it.
Whether a majority will prefer a therapy-framed prize that includes Knudsen; if so, the choice of whom she replaces has no clearly correct answer.
Whether the long-term safety and durability of the obesity indication will change how the achievement is judged in later years.
For B045, whether any three-person subset of the six credited names can be defended; I currently think none can.
For B040, whether Eshhar's absence from the credited names and Rosenberg's role can be resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal basis applies to B020 or to any shortlisted candidate. For the record I disclose a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann and a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, neither concerning a shortlisted candidate. Optogenetics is within my broad field of neuroscience, and I have not treated that as a conflict. I have not favoured it, and in this round I have moved away from proposing it. I have also noted Wahren-Herlenius's disclosure of field proximity on B034 and Svenningsson's note of past co-authorship with Perlmann.
